result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.percolation_threshold_analysis()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Perform percolation threshold analysis. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L15112-L15177){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.percolation_threshold_analysis( steps=20, trials=10, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Systematically removes nodes at different fractions and measures the relative size of the giant connected component (GCC) at each step. This helps identify the critical percolation threshold where the network fragments. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [steps]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[20]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of removal fractions to test. Results in `(steps + 1)` data points from `q=0.0` to `q=1.0`. [trials]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of random trials per step for averaging. More trials give smoother results but take longer. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducibility. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list of tuple]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(q, relative_gcc_size)` tuples where: - `q` is the fraction of nodes removed - `relative_gcc_size` is the average relative size of the giant connected component (GCC size / surviving nodes) ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Percolation theory studies what fraction of nodes you can remove before a graph fragments; the *percolation threshold* $q_c$ is the fraction at which the giant connected component vanishes. This routine samples the transition curve empirically by removing nodes at fractions $q = 0, \tfrac{1}{s}, \tfrac{2}{s}, \dots, 1$ and averaging the giant-component fraction over `trials` random draws at each $q$. Sharper transitions show up as steeper drops in the returned curve. For Erdős-Rényi random graphs the critical value falls near $q_c \approx 1 - 1/\langle k \rangle$ with $\langle k \rangle$ the average degree, a benchmark useful for spot-checking whether an empirical network is more or less robust than a random baseline. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Perform percolation threshold analysis: ::: {#074bfe8d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(50) results = graph.percolation_threshold_analysis(steps=10, trials=5) # Returns list of (q, relative_gcc_size) tuples # q=0.0: GCC=1.00, q=0.1: GCC=1.00, ... results ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(0.0, 1.0), (0.1, 1.0), (0.2, 1.0), (0.3, 1.0), (0.4, 1.0), (0.5, 1.0), (0.6, 1.0), (0.7, 1.0), (0.8, 1.0), (0.9, 1.0), (1.0, 0.0)] ``` ::: :::
